issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: Arthur had spent sixty-eight years moving through space with practiced grace, but the collision on Elm Street stopped him cold. The night he was walking home from his senior ballet workshop, a delivery truck hydroplaned across the wet pavement and struck him without warning. He remembered the sickening impact, the shatter of safety glass, and the terrifying weight of metal pressing against his chest. When the responders finally arrived, they took nearly forty minutes to extricate him, and the subsequent paperwork was a blur of misplaced forms and hollow assurances. Arthur’s dance career, built on precision and trust in his own physicality, fractured in that moment. What frightened him most was the quiet realization that the institutions and people designed to protect him had simply let him fall. In the months that followed, Arthur found that the crash refused to settle into a linear narrative. He felt like he was only remembering scattered fragments, with large, terrifying gaps in between, and when he tried deliberately to recall what happened, his mind simply went blank. His deep doubt about his own capacity to do the right thing caused him to dismiss his own recollections as faulty, leaving the gaps in his narrative even more pronounced. This inability to construct a clear story of the event did not leave him at peace; instead, the fragmented recall seeped into his sense of self, convincing him that he could not trust his own judgment or his body to function reliably. Because he no longer trusted his physical responses, every sudden noise on the street quickly triggered a jolted alarm. His belief that the world operated without warning directly fueled his hypervigilance, turning every unexpected sound into a potential catastrophe. This conviction quickly became the engine of his withdrawal. Telling himself that stepping outside would inevitably lead to harm he was powerless to prevent, Arthur stopped going out and began avoiding seeing the friends he had socialized with before the collision. He even carefully avoided thinking about anything discussed in therapy, treating every session prompt as a trap he might fail. Yet this retreat offered no escape from the fear itself. Because he kept his back to the wall in every room he entered, his nervous system remained locked in a state of perpetual readiness. By refusing to leave his apartment and face the ordinary world, he deprived himself of any chance to prove that outings were safe, and the unchallenged dread only grew louder, confirming his original fear that he was too broken to trust himself. The gaps in his recollection continued to shape his daily routine within his dimly lit apartment. He felt like he was only remembering parts of the crash, with the rest lost to a fog he could not pierce, and this persistent uncertainty bled into his present, amplifying the terror of sudden sounds. He came to believe that when anything took longer than expected, it was a sign of impending harm, a certainty that was made unbearable by his inability to deliberately access the memory of the event itself. His lack of trust in his own mind reinforced his negative appraisals, which then drove him to retreat further from the world. It was an exhausting, self-sustaining loop. Arthur finally sought help after his building manager found him sitting on the hardwood floor of his apartment, paralyzed by a loud delivery truck backfiring outside. He was most afraid that if he did not confront this paralysis, he would fade into isolation entirely, but he hoped that perhaps someone could help him finally piece the past together without losing himself in the process.
